opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that visual observations are incredibly rich and high-dimensional, and most of that richness is irrelevant to whatever you're actually trying to do. If a robot just watches the world with no purpose, it has no way of knowing which aspects of the image matter. Is it the lighting? The texture of the table? The position of the cup? From a pure perception standpoint, all of those are equally salient pixels.

Once you have a goal, that changes the problem fundamentally. The goal gives you a lens: it tells you which distinctions in the visual input actually make a difference to outcomes. If I'm trying to put the cup in the sink, then the cup's position and the gripper's relationship to it suddenly become the things worth representing, and the wallpaper doesn't. So the goal acts as a kind of filter that turns this overwhelming firehose of visual data into something structured.

There's also a nice self-supervision angle to this. With goal-conditioned learning, you can take any trajectory the robot happened to experience, even a failed one, and relabel it: "Well, I didn't reach the goal I was aiming for, but I did reach *this* state, so let me treat that as the goal and learn from it." That means every bit of experience becomes useful training signal for understanding how actions change the visual world. You're no longer relying on someone hand-engineering a reward function from pixels, which is notoriously hard.

And I think this mirrors something about how people and animals learn. We don't learn to see in some purely passive, task-agnostic way and then figure out how to act afterward. Perception and action develop together, and what we pay attention to is shaped by what we're trying to accomplish. So giving robots goals is, in a sense, giving them the same kind of grounding: a reason to care about some parts of the visual world over others, and a way to discover what those parts are through interaction rather than labels.

r001.rationale: The response says a goal directs attention to visual distinctions that affect the outcome, such as the cup’s position, while filtering out irrelevant details like wallpaper.

r002.rationale: It says people’s attention is shaped by their goals, but does not state that they can fail to notice something directly in front of them because it is irrelevant.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the hard part of learning from images isn't really the images themselves. The hard part is figuring out what in the image you should care about. A camera gives you, let's say, a few hundred thousand numbers every frame, and the vast majority of those numbers are irrelevant to whatever the robot is supposed to be doing. The lighting changed, there's a person walking in the background, the shadow moved. If you're just trying to model all of that, you're spending your capacity on stuff that doesn't matter.

What a goal does is it gives you a criterion for relevance. If I'm a robot and my job is to put the cup in the sink, then the question of what to pay attention to is answered by the task. The cup matters, the sink matters, the position of my gripper relative to the cup matters. The pattern on the wallpaper does not. And you don't have to hand-engineer that distinction. If you train the system end to end to accomplish the goal, the gradient signal effectively tells the perceptual part of the system which features are predictive of success and which ones aren't. So the goal acts as a filter on perception.

There's also a second thing, which I think is actually more subtle and maybe more important. When you have a goal, you get a lot of supervision essentially for free, because you can evaluate your own behavior. Did I get closer to the cup or not? Did the cup end up in the sink or not? That's a much richer and more grounded training signal than, say, trying to reconstruct the image pixel by pixel, which is what you'd be stuck doing with a purely unsupervised approach. And in the goal-conditioned setting specifically, you can go further and say: whatever state I happened to reach, I can treat that as the goal in hindsight, and now I have a labeled example of how to get there. So every trajectory, even the failed ones, becomes useful data about the relationship between what you see and what you can do.

So I'd summarize it as: the goal tells the robot what to look at, and it tells the robot how it's doing. Those two things together make the visual learning problem a lot more tractable than it looks if you think about it purely as a computer vision problem.

r001.rationale: The response says the goal determines what the robot should attend to, highlighting task-relevant objects and features while filtering out irrelevant details.

r002.rationale: It discusses irrelevant visual details for a robot, but does not state that people can fail to notice things directly in front of them because those things are irrelevant to their current goal.

astra-6.text:
Well, a goal gives you a way to decide which parts of the visual information matter. If you’re just trying to predict what a camera will see next, there are an enormous number of things you could spend your capacity on—the texture of the table, the shadows, what’s happening in the background. Some of those might be very difficult to predict, but completely irrelevant to what the robot needs to do.

If your goal is to pick up a cup, then what matters is where the cup is, how it’s oriented, where your hand is relative to it, and what happens when you make contact. You don’t necessarily have to reconstruct every pixel to understand those things.

So the goal provides a kind of organizing principle for learning a representation. Through trying to accomplish the task, the robot can learn which distinctions in its observations actually affect success. That doesn’t make visual learning easy, but it gives you a signal for what you should be learning about.

r001.rationale: It says the goal helps determine which visual details matter and gives the cup’s position, orientation, and contact as task-relevant examples.

r002.rationale: It describes irrelevant visual details for a robot, but does not say that people can fail to notice things directly in front of them when those things are irrelevant to their goal.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a goal gives you a way to decide which parts of the visual information actually matter. An image contains an enormous amount of detail, but most of it might be irrelevant to what you're trying to do. If you're trying to pick up a cup, the position of the cup relative to your hand matters a lot. The pattern on the tablecloth probably doesn't.

The tricky thing is that you don't necessarily know ahead of time what you can ignore. But if you're learning to accomplish a goal, that provides a signal for learning the representation itself. You can learn to extract the information that helps you choose successful actions, rather than trying to understand every pixel equally well.

And acting helps, too. The robot can move its hand, see what changes, and gradually learn which visual features correspond to things it can control. So the goal doesn't make vision easy, but it gives the learning process some structure: what do I need to understand about this scene in order to do the thing I'm trying to do?

r001.rationale: It says a goal helps the robot identify which visual details matter for its task and learn features useful for successful actions.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of irrelevant visual details, but does not state that people can fail to notice things directly in front of them.
